'''Madeleine M. Joullié''' (born March 29, 1927) is an American-Brazilian organic chemist. She was the first woman to join the [[University of Pennsylvania]] chemistry faculty as well as the first female [[organic chemist]] to be appointed to a [[tenure track]] position in a major American university. She was one of the first affirmative action officers at the University of Pennsylvania. She has a distinguished record as a teacher of both undergraduate and graduate-level organic chemistry, and as a mentor of students.<ref name=Semple/>

Joullié is also an active researcher in organic chemistry who has published three textbooks of organic chemistry, more than 18 review articles, and more than 300 scientific papers.<ref name=Semple/> Her work in synthesizing organic compounds such as [[tilorone]], [[furanomycin]], and numerous [[cyclopeptides]] has led to the development of [[antibiotic]] and [[antiviral drugs]].<ref name=Encyclopedia>{{cite book|last=Oakes|first=Elizabeth H.|title=Encyclopedia of world scientists|year=2007|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=978-1438118826|pages=381–383|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA382|edition=Rev.}}</ref>  Joullié has received numerous awards, including the 1978 [[Garvan Medal]] from the [[American Chemical Society]], in recognition of her accomplishments in teaching and research.<ref name=OralHistory/>

==Early life==

Madeleine Joullié was born in Paris, France.<ref name=Encyclopedia/> Her father, an international businessman, soon moved to [[Rio de Janeiro]], [[Brazil]], where she attended the [[Lycée Français]]. The family also lived briefly in [[São Paulo]]. There she attended a private school, the {{Interlanguage link multi|Liceu Rio Branco|pt|3=Colégio Rio Branco}}.<ref name="OralHistory"/>

Joullié moved to the United States to study in 1946.<ref name=Quote/> She obtained a B.S. degree in chemistry from [[Simmons College]], a women's college in [[Boston]], in 1949.<ref name=OralHistory/> Then she moved to [[Philadelphia]], where she was the only full-time female graduate student in chemistry at the University of Pennsylvania. There weren't even bathrooms for women in the chemistry building.<ref name=AlumniMagazine>{{cite journal|title=Chemistry Professor Madeleine Joullié An Appreciation|journal=School of Arts and Science Alumni Magazine|year=2003|url=https://www.sas.upenn.edu/sasalum/newsltr/spring03/joullie.html|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref> She earned an M.S. from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1950 and a Ph.D. in 1953.<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Madeleine M. Joullié |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/joulli%C3%A9-madeleine-m|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="OralHistory">{{cite book|first=James H. |last=Bohning|title=Madeleine M. Joullié, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James H. Bohning at the Chemical Heritage Foundation, 23 April 1991 |date=23 April 1991 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/joullie_mm_0092_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Science History Institute|Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref>
She worked with [[Allan R. Day]], who inspired Joullié as both a researcher and a teacher.<ref name=Day>{{cite web|last=Joullié|first=Madeleine|title=Allan R. Day: In memory of a great teacher|url=http://www.pocclub.org/POCC_Awards_ARDay.html|publisher=Philadelphia Organic Chemists' Club (POCC)|access-date=9 May 2014|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924074657/http://www.pocclub.org/POCC_Awards_ARDay.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Also at the university, Joullié met Richard E. Prange (1932–2008), a condensed matter theorist in the physics department.<ref name=OralHistory/><ref name=Prange>{{cite web|title=Richard E. Prange: 1932 – 2008|url=http://umdphysics.umd.edu/component/content/article/240.html|publisher=[[University of Maryland]]|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref> They married in 1959.<ref name=Encyclopedia/>

==Career==
In 1953, Madeleine Joullié joined the University of Pennsylvania chemistry faculty, the first woman to do so.<ref name=OralHistory/> Originally in a non-tenure-track position, Joullié  taught undergraduate organic chemistry five days a week and ran the lab. In her first five years, none of the graduate students would work with her, so she carried out research in collaboration with undergraduates. As more women entered the department, first female  and later male graduate students began to work with her.<ref name=AlumniMagazine/>

Joullié received a Fulbright scholarship to lecture at the University of Brazil (1965).  While there, she wrote a textbook in Portuguese on heterocyclic chemistry.<ref name=OralHistory/> She has also been a visiting professor at Columbia University (1968), CRNS (Grenoble, France, 1987), the University of California at Santa Barbara (1989), and Cambridge, England (1997), but the majority of her career has been spent at the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name=Group>{{cite web|title=Joullié Group University of Pennsylvania|url=https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~mjoullie/mmj.html|publisher=University of Pennsylvania|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref> Joullié became a full professor in 1974.<ref name=OralHistory/>

===Community involvement===
Joullié was active in the safety committee at UPenn, helping to identify and enforce safe work guidelines for the chemistry department.<ref name=Safety>{{cite web|last=Domush|first=Hilary|title=First Person: Madeleine Joullié|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/media/periodic-tabloid/archive/2012-07-17-first-person-madeleine-joullie.aspx|publisher=Chemical Heritage Foundation|access-date=9 May 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712021339/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/media/periodic-tabloid/archive/2012-07-17-first-person-madeleine-joullie.aspx|archive-date=July 12, 2016}}</ref>

In 1970, Joullié and [[Mildred Cohn]] worked on the Committee on the Status of Women, which gathered data and documented the second-class status of women at Penn. The percentage of women holding faculty positions was far below the percentage of qualified women Ph.D.'s, and those women who had positions held lower rank, received lower salaries, and waited longer for promotion.<ref name=AlumniMagazine/> The committee developed affirmative action guidelines, supporting the university's efforts to recruit more women and minority faculty.<ref name=OralHistory/>

Later in the 1970s, dean [[Vartan Gregorian]] appointed her as one of the first affirmative action officers at the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name=Semple/><ref name=AlumniMagazine/>  Between 1976 and 1980, Joullié reviewed the hiring and promotions processes of the School of Arts and Science, comparing resumes of male and female candidates. On some occasions, when she felt that qualified women had been ignored in the hiring process, she flatly refused to sign off on new hires. Her effectiveness in the position led Provost [[Eliot Stellar]] to appoint her as the chair of the university's Council for Equal Opportunity, overseeing affirmative action in all departments.<ref name=AlumniMagazine/> Of her affirmative action activities, Joullié says:

"I served in that role for seven years, without help, extra pay, or teaching relief... It was not a pleasant job, but it did produce results. The School of Arts and Sciences was so successful with their affirmative action program that I was then asked by the provost to chair the Council for Equal Opportunity to oversee the affirmative action programs of all the schools at Penn."<ref name=Quote/>

Described by professor Helen Davies as "fearless and formidable",<ref name=AlumniMagazine/> Joullié is credited as having played a key role in creating a culture of equality for women at the university.<ref name=Quote>{{cite web|title=Notes from an Interview with Madeleine Joullie|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/women-in-chemistry/madeleine-joullie.aspx|publisher=Chemical Heritage Foundation|access-date=9 May 2014|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712185019/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/women-in-chemistry/madeleine-joullie.aspx|archive-date=July 12, 2016}}</ref> Joullié also helped the [[American Chemical Society]] to develop professional guidelines for chemists.<ref name=OralHistory/>

===Scientific achievements===
Early in her career, her Ph.D. advisor, Allan R. Day, interested her in [[heterocyclic compound]]s, and she did early work with aromatic and heterocyclic scaffolds and fluorinated heterocycles. She also did significant research on  heterocyclic ketones in the 1970s, collaborating with Peter Yates of the [[University of Toronto]], and receiving the 1972 ACS Philadelphia Section Award.<ref name=Semple/> In the early 1970s, she successfully synthesized [[tilorone]], an interferon inducer which helps to protect cells.<ref name=Encyclopedia/>

Since then, much of Joullié's research has focused on the synthesis of natural products. In 1980, she reported the first asymmetric total synthesis of the antibiotic [[Furanomycin|(+)-furanomycin]], the first use of the [[Ugi reaction|Ugi 4CC]] in the synthesis of a [[Non-proteinogenic amino acids|non-proteinogenic amino acid]]. She helped to develop methodologies for [[aromatic substitution]], and introduced the term "[[Chirality (chemistry)|chirality]] transfer". Her subsequent work has led to the total synthesis of several natural products, including [[muscarine]], [[geiparvarin]], [[ascofuranone]], [[furanomycin]], and dihydromauritine A.<ref name=Semple/>

Working with [[Judah Folkman]] at [[Harvard Medical School]] and [[Paul B. Weisz]] at the University of Pennsylvania, Joullié helped to synthesize [[Cyclodextrin|beta-cyclodextrin sulfate]], a ring-shaped sugar molecule that attaches to the walls of growing blood vessels. By capturing and delivering cortisone molecules, it decreases the growth of new capillaries. Chemotherapies can thus target aberrant [[angiogenesis]], the growth of new blood vessels, and restrict the growth of malignant tumours. Joullié's specialized compounds made  Folkman's original treatments 100 to 1000 times more potent. Beta-cyclodextrin sulfate is also useful in limiting [[restenosis]], growth of cells on artery walls that can lead to blockages at the site of surgical procedures.<ref name=AlumniMagazine/>

Another particularly interesting area of research has involved the [[Didemnin]] class of macrocyclic depsipeptide. Derived from a marine [[tunicate]] of the family [[Didemnidae]], didemnins exhibit antitumor, antiviral and immunosuppressive qualities. Joullié's asymmetric total synthesis of didemnin B in 1990 was a landmark event leading to fundamental contributions to both the chemistry and biology of this intriguing class of natural products. Didemnin B was the first marine natural product to be used in clinical trials against cancer.<ref name=Semple>{{cite journal|last=Semple|first=J. Edward|title=A Tribute to Prof. Madeleine Joullie|journal=Arkivoc|date=14 July 2006|volume=2007|issue=12|pages=1–6|doi=10.3998/ark.5550190.0008.c01|doi-access=free|hdl=2027/spo.5550190.0008.c01|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Joullié has produced several didemnin analogs. She has also developed probe molecules that can trace didemnins, allowing researchers to more effectively study their biological activities.<ref name=AlumniMagazine/>

Another area of research has been [[ninhydrin]] analogs. Joullié's lab has developed compounds with enhanced chromogenic and [[Fluorescence|fluorogenic]] properties, useful in fingerprinting and forensic science.<ref name=Semple/> Joullié was asked  by the [[United States Secret Service]] to help in developing [[fingerprint]] reagents. Fingerprint chemicals must be non-toxic and can't damage sensitive evidence, as well as meeting other criteria. Joullié, with students Olga Petrovskaia and Diane Hauze, developed and patented a class of compounds called [[1,3-Indandione|indanediones]].<ref name=Gazette>{{cite news|title=How A Chemist Found Prints Charming|url=https://thepenngazette.com/how-a-chemist-found-prints-charming/|access-date=9 May 2014|newspaper=The Pennsylvania Gazette|year=2001}}</ref> Like ninhydrins, indanediones react with amino acids from the oil on people's fingertips.<ref name=Gazette/>  They have the advantages of being cheaper to produce, easier to use, and more sensitive, providing more clarity and sharper contrast.<ref name=Avery>{{cite news|last=Avery|first=Ron|title=She's A Queen Among Prints|url=http://articles.philly.com/1991-06-03/news/25786922_1_fingerprint-work-analogs-new-compounds|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517115346/http://articles.philly.com/1991-06-03/news/25786922_1_fingerprint-work-analogs-new-compounds|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 17, 2014|access-date=9 May 2014|newspaper=Philadelphia Daily News|date=3 June 1991}}</ref>  Indanediones are standardly used in the first stage of forensic identification of latent fingerprints.<ref name=Indanediones>{{cite video|title=Sequential Processing 2010 : 01 : History of Indanedione|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5xu_6VpGEu0|work=Sequential Processing of Documents For Fingerprints|publisher=NFSTC|accessdate=August 2, 2013}}</ref>

==Awards==
Madeleine M. Joullié has received a substantial number of awards, including the following:
* [[John Scott Medal]] (2015)
* Edward Leete Award (2009)<ref name=Leete>{{cite web|title=Edward Leete Award|url=http://www.organicdivision.org/?nd=p_leete_award|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref>
* Arthur C. Cope Senior Scholar Award (2002) from the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name=Cope>{{cite news|last=Byrum|first=Allison|title=Philadelphian wins national organic chemistry award|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2002-08/acs-pwn080802.php|access-date=9 May 2014|newspaper=American Chemical Society Press Release|date=13 August 2002|archive-date=19 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140519192642/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2002-08/acs-pwn080802.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Distinguished Achievement Award University of Pennsylvania Graduate Student Associate and [[Phi Lambda Upsilon]] (1999)
* [[ACS Award for Encouraging Women into Careers in the Chemical Sciences]] (1998)<ref name=Careers>{{cite web|title=ACS Award for Encouraging Women into Careers in the Chemical Sciences|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-encouraging-women-into-careers-in-the-chemical-sciences.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref>
* H. Martin Friedmann Lectureship, Rutgers University (1995)
* Henry Hill Award (1994)<ref name=Hill>{{cite journal|title=Madeleine Joullié wins Henry Hill Award|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=5 September 1994|volume=72|issue=36|pages=45–46|doi=10.1021/cen-v072n036.p045|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Philadelphia Organic Chemist's Club Award (1994)<ref name=POCC>{{cite web|title=POCC Awards|url=http://www.pocclub.org/POCC_Awards.html|publisher=Philadelphia Organic Chemists' Club (POCC)|access-date=9 May 2014|archive-date=24 February 2011|archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20110224071434/http://www.pocclub.org/POCC_Awards.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Second Annual Association of American Women in Science, Philadelphia Chapter Award (1991)
* Lindback Award for Distinguished Teaching (1991)
* American Institute of Chemists 34th Annual Scroll Award (1988)<ref name=Almanac>{{cite journal|title=Honors &... Other Things|journal=University of Pennsylvania Almanac|date=26 May 1987|volume=33|issue=36|page=2|url=https://almanac.upenn.edu/archive/v33pdf/n36/052687.pdf|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref>
* American Cyanamid Faculty Award (1984)
* [[Garvan Medal]] (1978)<ref name=Garvan>{{cite web|title=Francis P. Garvan-John M. Olin Medal|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/francis-p-garvan-john-m-olin-medal.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=9 May 2014}}</ref>
